plan.estimand: Hazard ratio for survival comparison (treatment vs control)
plan.hypothesis: Two-sided test of equality: H₀: HR = 1 vs H₁: HR ≠ 1
assumptions: Two-sided log-rank test at significance level α = 0.05
Hazard ratio of 0.7 represents the true treatment effect
Event probabilities are marginal probabilities at the study endpoint
Freedman approximation is the underlying analytic model
scientific_notes: Freedman (1982) approximation for log-rank test power uses the number of events and is derived from the normal approximation to the hypergeometric distribution under alternative hypothesis
powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default implements this formula; execution will verify the exact computation
The event probabilities provided (0.3707 and 0.4890) represent the marginal probability of event occurrence over the study period

answer.summary: Power calculation for two-sided log-rank test comparing survival curves using the Freedman approximation. With 200 participants per group (400 total), hazard ratio 0.7 (treatment vs control), event probabilities 0.3707 (treatment) and 0.4890 (control), and significance level α=0.05, the achieved power is 0.6383 (63.83%).
answer.method: Freedman approximation for log-rank test (Freedman 1982, as implemented in powerSurvEpi::powerCT.default). The formula is: power = Φ(√(km)|RR−1|/(kRR+1) − z_{1−α/2}), where k=n_E/n_C (allocation ratio), m=n_E·p_E+n_C·p_C (expected total events), RR is the hazard ratio, and Φ is the standard normal CDF.
assumptions: Two-sided log-rank test at significance level α = 0.05
Hazard ratio 0.7 represents the true treatment effect
Event probabilities (0.3707 treatment, 0.4890 control) are marginal probabilities over the maximum study follow-up period
Underlying Cox proportional hazards model with constant hazard ratio
Normal approximation via Freedman method is valid (assumes sufficiently large sample size)
limitations: The Freedman approximation assumes the central limit theorem is valid; appropriateness depends on the observed number of events (171.94 expected)
The formula does not account for specific censoring distributions, only marginal event probabilities
No adjustment for multiple comparisons, interim analyses, or departures from proportional hazards assumption
Marginal event probabilities must be provided; the calculation does not derive them from survival curves or follow-up times

# Install and load powerSurvEpi
if (!require("powerSurvEpi", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("powerSurvEpi", repos = "https://cran.r-project.org")
}
library(powerSurvEpi)

# Study parameters
n_per_group <- 200
total_n <- n_per_group * 2
hr <- 0.7  # Hazard ratio (treatment vs control)
alpha <- 0.05
event_prob_treatment <- 0.3707
event_prob_control <- 0.4890

# Calculate expected number of events
n_events_treatment <- n_per_group * event_prob_treatment
n_events_control <- n_per_group * event_prob_control
total_events <- n_events_treatment + n_events_control

cat("Study Design:\n")
cat("  Sample size per group:", n_per_group, "\n")
cat("  Total sample size:", total_n, "\n")
cat("  Total expected events:", total_events, "\n")
cat("  Expected events (treatment):", n_events_treatment, "\n")
cat("  Expected events (control):", n_events_control, "\n")
cat("  Hazard ratio:", hr, "\n")
cat("  Significance level (α):", alpha, "\n")
cat("  Two-sided test\n\n")

# Use powerCT.default with Freedman approximation
# Parameters:
# - type: "two.sided" for two-sided test
# - alpha: significance level
# - beta: 1 - power (we'll solve for power, so we leave as NULL and check return)
# - hr: hazard ratio
# - n: total sample size (we use n_per_group * 2 for total)
# - p_event_ctrl: event probability in control group
# - p_event_trt: event probability in treatment group

# powerCT.default uses Freedman approximation
power_result <- powerCT.default(
  type = "two.sided",
  alpha = alpha,
  beta = NULL,  # We want to compute power (1 - beta)
  hr = hr,
  n = total_n,
  p_event_ctrl = event_prob_control,
  p_event_trt = event_prob_treatment
)

cat("Power Calculation Result:\n")
print(power_result)

# Extract the power value
power <- 1 - power_result$beta
cat("\nComputed Power:", power, "\n")

# Return result in required format
results_json <- jsonlite::toJSON(
  list(
    results = list(
      list(metric = "power", value = power, unit = "probability")
    )
  ),
  auto_unbox = TRUE,
  digits = 15
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", results_json, "\n")

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     This is an implementation of the power calculation method
     described in Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006). The method
     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     Suppose we want to compare the survival curves between an
     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

                      h(t|X_1)=h_0(t)\exp(beta_1 X_1).

     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the

     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =

     standard normal distribution N(0, 1), Phi is the cumulative
     distribution function (CDF) of N(0, 1).

     The power formula assumes that the central-limit theorem is valid
     and hence is appropriate for large samples.

library(powerSurvEpi)

# Show the underlying formula implementation
cat("Underlying function (powerCT.default0):\n")
cat(capture.output(print(powerCT.default0)), "\n\n")

# Manual verification of the Freedman formula
nE <- 200
nC <- 200
pE <- 0.3707
pC <- 0.4890
RR <- 0.7
alpha <- 0.05

# Calculate components as per Freedman formula
k <- nE / nC  # ratio of group sizes
m <- nE * pE + nC * pC  # total expected events

cat("Freedman Approximation Verification:\n")
cat("  k (nE/nC):", k, "\n")
cat("  m (nE*pE + nC*pC):", m, "\n")

# Formula: power = Phi(sqrt(k*m) * |RR - 1| / (k*RR + 1) - z_{1-alpha/2})
# where Phi is the standard normal CDF

z_critical <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
cat("  z_{1-alpha/2} (critical value for two-sided α=0.05):", z_critical, "\n")

# Calculate the test statistic component
test_stat <- sqrt(k * m) * abs(RR - 1) / (k * RR + 1)
cat("  sqrt(k*m) * |RR - 1| / (k*RR + 1):", test_stat, "\n")

# Power calculation
power_manual <- pnorm(test_stat - z_critical)
cat("  Power (manual calculation): Phi(", test_stat, "-", z_critical, ") =", power_manual, "\n\n")

# Compare with function result
power_function <- powerCT.default(nE = nE, nC = nC, pE = pE, pC = pC, RR = RR, alpha = alpha)
cat("Power from powerCT.default():", power_function, "\n")
cat("Difference:", abs(power_manual - power_function), "\n")

# Install and load powerSurvEpi

  install.packages("powerSurvEpi", repos = "https://cran.r-project.org")

library(powerSurvEpi)

# Study parameters
n_per_group <- 200
total_n <- n_per_group * 2
hr <- 0.7  # Hazard ratio (treatment vs control)
alpha <- 0.05
event_prob_treatment <- 0.3707
event_prob_control <- 0.4890

# Calculate expected number of events
n_events_treatment <- n_per_group * event_prob_treatment
n_events_control <- n_per_group * event_prob_control
total_events <- n_events_treatment + n_events_control

cat("Study Design:\n")
cat("  Sample size per group:", n_per_group, "\n")
cat("  Total sample size:", total_n, "\n")
cat("  Total expected events:", total_events, "\n")
cat("  Expected events (treatment):", n_events_treatment, "\n")
cat("  Expected events (control):", n_events_control, "\n")
cat("  Hazard ratio:", hr, "\n")
cat("  Significance level (α):", alpha, "\n")
cat("  Two-sided test\n\n")

# Use powerCT.default with Freedman approximation
# Parameters:
# - type: "two.sided" for two-sided test
# - alpha: significance level
# - beta: 1 - power (we'll solve for power, so we leave as NULL and check return)
# - hr: hazard ratio
# - n: total sample size (we use n_per_group * 2 for total)
# - p_event_ctrl: event probability in control group
# - p_event_trt: event probability in treatment group

# powerCT.default uses Freedman approximation
power_result <- powerCT.default(
  type = "two.sided",
  alpha = alpha,
  beta = NULL,  # We want to compute power (1 - beta)
  hr = hr,
  n = total_n,
  p_event_ctrl = event_prob_control,
  p_event_trt = event_prob_treatment
)

cat("Power Calculation Result:\n")
print(power_result)

# Extract the power value
power <- 1 - power_result$beta
cat("\nComputed Power:", power, "\n")

# Return result in required format
results_json <- jsonlite::toJSON(
  list(
    results = list(
      list(metric = "power", value = power, unit = "probability")
    )
  ),
  auto_unbox = TRUE,
  digits = 15
)

cat("\nPOWER_AGENT_RESULT=", results_json, "\n")

_ D_ e_ s_ c_ r_ i_ p_ t_ i_ o_ n:

     Power calculation for the Comparison of Survival Curves Between
     Two Groups under the Cox Proportional-Hazards Model for clinical
     trials.

_ U_ s_ a_ g_ e:

     powerCT.default(nE, 
                     nC, 
                     pE, 
                     pC, 
                     RR, 
                     alpha = 0.05)
     
_ A_ r_ g_ u_ m_ e_ n_ t_ s:

      nE: integer. number of participants in the experimental group.

      nC: integer. number of participants in the control group.

      pE: numeric. probability of failure in group E (experimental
          group) over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      pC: numeric. probability of failure in group C (control group)
          over the maximum time period of the study (t years).

      RR: numeric. postulated hazard ratio.

   alpha: numeric. type I error rate.

_ D_ e_ t_ a_ i_ l_ s:

     This is an implementation of the power calculation method
     described in Section 14.12 (page 807) of Rosner (2006). The method
     was proposed by Freedman (1982).

     Suppose we want to compare the survival curves between an
     experimental group (E) and a control group (C) in a clinical trial
     with a maximum follow-up of t years.  The Cox proportional hazards
     regression model is assumed to have the form:

                      h(t|X_1)=h_0(t)\exp(beta_1 X_1).                  
     
     Let n_E be the number of participants in the E group and n_C be
     the number of participants in the C group.  We wish to test the
     hypothesis H0: RR=1 versus H1: RR not equal to 1, where
     RR=\exp(beta_1)=underlying hazard ratio for the E group versus the
     C group. Let RR be the postulated hazard ratio, alpha be the
     significance level. Assume that the test is a two-sided test. If
     the ratio of participants in group E compared to group C =
     n_E/n_C=k, then the power of the test is

             power=Phi(sqrt{k*m}*|RR-1|/(k*RR+1)-z_{1-alpha/2}),        
     
     where

                             m=n_E p_E+n_C p_C,                         
     
     and z_{1-alpha/2} is the 100 (1-alpha/2)-th percentile of the
     standard normal distribution N(0, 1), Phi is the cumulative
     distribution function (CDF) of N(0, 1).

     The power of the test.

_ N_ o_ t_ e:

     The power formula assumes that the central-limit theorem is valid
     and hence is appropriate for large samples.
